ta-l1d15q3-d1e3498.summary: Transitional paragraph turning to mission from the side of the sender, in two articles: whether any person gives, sends, or proceeds from himself, and whether the Son is sent by the Spirit.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3510.summary: First objection that no person gives or sends himself. A giver always seems to have authority over what is given, and no person has authority over himself.
claims: A giver has authority over what is given.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3513.summary: Second objection. Lombard said (Dist. 14) that humans cannot give the Spirit because he does not proceed from them, and no person proceeds from himself, otherwise he would be his own principle.
claims: One can give only what proceeds from oneself.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3516.summary: Third objection. Mission implies the going out of the one sent from the sender (q. 1, a. 2), and no person can send himself in this way.
claims: Mission implies going out from the sender.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3520.summary: Fourth objection. Procession principally implies a person's relation to the principle from which it is distinguished, and no person is distinguished from himself, so none proceeds from himself.
claims: Procession implies distinction from the principle.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3523.summary: Fifth objection. The preposition 'from' (a) implies the relation of a principle, and nothing is its own principle. So even if a person sends himself, he should not be said to be sent from himself.
claims: 'A' implies a principle.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3526.summary: Sed contra from Augustine: as to be begotten is for the Son to be from the Father, so for the Son to be known to be from the Father is for him to be sent. That knowledge can be caused by the Son, so the Son's mission can be from the Son.
claims: Mission is being known to be from another, which the Son himself can cause.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3532.summary: Second sed contra from Lombard's text.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3535.summary: Thomas's determination, distinguishing giving, mission, and procession. (1) Giving implies only that what is given is freely had by the one given it. Having can be as one freely has oneself or something in oneself, or as one has a possession under lordship. Giving implies authority over what is given only when specified to having by lordship, which does not exist in God. So the essence can be given, as the Father gives his essence to the Son, and a person can give himself, with at most a conceptual distinction of giver and given. A person gives himself and is given by himself, simply. (2) Mission is harder, as the diversity of opinions shows. Some say 'the Spirit sends himself' is false, that Lombard's arguments fail because mission includes a notion, and that the Son's sending himself into flesh is a special case; texts saying the Spirit sends himself should be glossed as 'the effect by which he is known to be from another is from the Spirit'. Praepositinus and William of Auxerre say mission is sometimes proper, implying distinction from the sender, and sometimes improper, for influence or giving, in which sense the Spirit sends himself. Thomas sides with those who say the Spirit properly sends himself. Mission implies being from another, by the authority it implies, and an effect by which the Spirit is in a creature in a new way. A conjoined predicate said by way of being requires both parts ('Socrates is a white man'), but said by way of becoming requires only one part to be in becoming ('Socrates has now become a white man' needs only that he became white). Moreover, on the side of the maker it suffices that the maker makes one part ('the painter makes the wall white'). Mission implies a kind of making, conceptual only and terminating in a conceptual relation, as God 'became our refuge': 'the Spirit is sent' means he who is from another has come to exist in the creature through grace. So the Father cannot be sent, not being from another. On the sender's side, to send the Spirit is to make him who exists from another be in someone by a new relation. Any person who does this is said to send him, even if not his principle. Since the whole Trinity makes the Spirit be in someone newly, through the gift conferred by the whole Trinity, the whole Trinity sends the Spirit, and in this sense he sends himself and is sent by himself. (3) 'The Spirit proceeds from himself' is less proper than 'is sent by himself', but since temporal procession implies a new relation to the creature and all newness implies some making, it too can be granted in the same sense.
claims: A divine person can give himself, since giving implies no authority except under lordship.
The Spirit properly sends himself, since to send is to make the one who is from another be newly in a creature, which the whole Trinity does.
The Father cannot be sent because he is not from another, though he sends.
Temporal procession 'from himself' can be granted in the same sense, less properly.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3544.summary: Reply to the first objection. Giving does not imply authority over what is given except when what is given is had by way of lordship, and there is no such giving in God.
claims: Giving implies authority only under lordship.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3548.summary: Reply to the second objection. Humans effect neither of the things implied in mission: they do not confer grace, and the Spirit does not proceed from them. So humans can in no way send the Spirit.
claims: Humans can in no way send the Spirit.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3551.summary: Reply to the third objection. Mission implies not only going out but also being in the creature by a new relation. As to going out, the Spirit is not referred to himself as principle, but as to the whole compound he is: he makes himself, who exists from another, be in someone by a new relation, by reason of the perfection he confers.
claims: As to the compound of origin and new presence, the Spirit is principle of his own mission.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3554.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. Although procession implies only a relation to the person from whom he has being, temporal procession also implies a relation to the creature into which he proceeds, and by reason of this he is said to proceed temporally from himself, as he is sent by himself.
claims: Temporal procession from himself is grounded in the relation to the creature.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3557.summary: Reply to the fifth objection. Though the Spirit is not simply his own principle, he makes himself, existing from another, be in someone by a new relation, so the whole compound is referred to him as principle by reason of one part only.
claims: The Spirit is principle of his mission by reason of the new presence alone.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3569.summary: First argument that the Spirit does not give or send the Son. Augustine says the Son's going out from the Father and coming into the world is his being sent by the Father, and the Son does not go out from the Spirit.
claims: Mission is going out from the sender.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3572.summary: Second argument. The Spirit stands to the Son as the Son to the Father, and the Son in no way sends the Father.
claims: The Son does not send the Father.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3575.summary: Sed contra from Isaiah 48:16, 'the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit', glossed of the Son.
claims: The Son is sent by the Father and the Spirit.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3582.summary: Second sed contra from Ambrose: the Son was given by the Father (Isa. 9:6) and, I dare say, by the Spirit, since he was sent by the Spirit.
claims: Ambrose: the Son is given and sent by the Spirit.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3591.summary: Thomas's determination. Some distinguish three missions of the Son: into flesh, into the mind, and to preach. They say only the last, which belongs to Christ by reason of his human nature, is from the Spirit, while the first two concern the Son's person itself and are from the Father alone, since the Spirit has authority only over the assumed nature. But, as shown, mission does not necessarily require authority in the sender over the one sent, only efficiency regarding that by which he is said to be sent. So the Spirit and the whole Trinity sent the Son in every mission, especially since Augustine expressly says, of the mission in the flesh, that he could not be sent by the Father without the Spirit, since the Father sent him when he made him from a woman, which he did not do without the Spirit.
claims: The Son is sent by the Spirit and the whole Trinity in every mission, since sending requires only efficiency over the effect.
The threefold distinction limiting the Spirit's sending to the mission to preach is rejected.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3600.summary: Reply to the first argument. When the Father is said to send the Son, authority over the one sent is understood in the sender, not as sender but as Father, so the Son's being sent by the Father is his going out from the Father. No authority is shown when the Son is said to send himself or the Spirit sends him, so his being sent by himself or by the Spirit is not his going out from himself or the Spirit.
claims: Only in the Father's sending is authority of origin implied; the Son's sending by himself or the Spirit implies only efficiency.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3603.summary: Reply to the second argument. The Son cannot send the Father because the Father cannot be sent, not being from another. If he were from another, he could be sent and the Son would send him.
claims: The Father cannot be sent, since he is not from another.

ta-l1d15q3-d1e3612.summary: An expositio textus on Lombard's two arguments that the Spirit gives himself, one from power and one from operation, both common to the three persons. It seems they fail, since the Father can beget and begets while the Son cannot and does not, without any division of power or operation. Thomas answers that if giving and temporal procession were only by the relation of eternal origin, the arguments would fail, as with generation. But because they also include efficiency regarding effects in the creature, which are common to the whole Trinity, the arguments conclude necessarily.
claims: Lombard's arguments hold because mission includes an effect in creatures produced by the whole Trinity.

ta-l1d15q3-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Question 3 introduces mission from the side of the sender: whether a person can give, send, or proceed from himself, and whether the Spirit sends the Son.

ta-l1d15q3-Dd1e3502.summary: Article 1 asks whether a person can give, send, or proceed from himself. Thomas holds that a person can give himself simply, since giving implies authority only under lordship, which is absent in God. He then sides with those who hold that the Spirit properly sends himself. Mission compounds being from another with being newly present in the creature, and since a compound said by way of becoming requires only one part to be made, to send is to make the one who is from another be newly in a creature. The whole Trinity does this through its common gift. The Father cannot be sent, not being from another, and temporal procession 'from himself' can be granted in the same sense, less properly.
claims: A person can give himself, and the Spirit properly sends himself; the whole Trinity sends.
The Father cannot be sent.

ta-l1d15q3-Dd1e3561.summary: Article 2 asks whether the Spirit sends the Son. Rejecting the view that the Spirit sends the Son only in his mission to preach, Thomas holds that the Spirit and the whole Trinity send the Son in every mission, including the incarnation. Sending requires only efficiency over the effect, not authority of origin. Authority belongs only to the Father's sending, as Father, and the Father cannot be sent.
claims: The Spirit and the whole Trinity send the Son in every mission.
Only the Father's sending implies authority of origin.

ta-l1d15q3-Dd1e3607.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 15 defends Lombard's arguments that the Spirit gives himself. They hold because giving and mission include effects in creatures, which are common to the whole Trinity.
claims: Mission includes effects common to the Trinity.

ta-l1d15q3.summary: Quaestio 3 of Book I, Distinction 15 treats mission from the side of the sender. Article 1 holds that a divine person can give himself, since giving in God implies no lordship. It holds that the Spirit properly sends himself: mission compounds being from another with being newly present in a creature, and the whole Trinity brings about the latter through its common gift. The Father, not being from another, cannot be sent. Article 2 holds that the Spirit and the whole Trinity send the Son in every mission, including the incarnation, since sending requires only efficiency over the effect. Authority of origin belongs only to the Father's sending. The Expositio defends Lombard's arguments on the same ground of common operation toward creatures.
claims: The Spirit sends himself and the whole Trinity sends both Son and Spirit.
The Father sends but cannot be sent.
Sending requires efficiency over the effect; only the Father's sending implies authority of origin.
